notes: Reconciled from coder A and coder B. All three documents are university-layer AIEAC web pages (ai.fsu.edu); no school, computing or course documents were collected. FSU's formal policy is still pending Faculty Senate/Provost review, so every page delegates the decision to instructors. The faculty and student pages repeat some sentences from the integrity page and each page is coded on its own. One unit is UNCOVERED (educative-sanctions principle).

documents.title: Academic Integrity (AI guideline)
documents.stance_why: The guideline says "Whether you determine AI use is appropriate in your course or not", so the decision rests with each instructor, and the page only requires clear communication and use of the Academic Honor Policy; it sets no university-wide permission or ban.
documents.summary: Official AIEAC academic integrity guideline for faculty: instructors set and communicate AI rules in syllabi, treat misuse via the Honor Policy, avoid AI detectors, and follow an early-intervention process with students.

units.why: The guideline sentence tells instructors to set expectations and define acceptable AI use "in your course syllabus and materials", so it is a communication rule for instructors (course-start, should); P09 fits because it requires AI expectations in the syllabus.
units.anchor: setting expectations and clearly defining acceptable AI use in your course syllabus and materials

units.why: "Whether you determine AI use is appropriate in your course or not" leaves the allow/ban decision to each instructor, so it is a delegation rule (P04), not a default stance.
units.anchor: Whether you determine AI use is appropriate in your course or not
units.policy: Each instructor determines whether AI use is appropriate in their course.

units.why: The same sentence says "clearly communicating your AI policies with students in your course syllabus and assignment instructions" is expected of instructors regardless of the decision; this is a distinct communication rule coded as P09 (the delegation part is the previous unit).
units.anchor: clearly communicating your AI policies with students in your course syllabus and assignment instructions

units.why: "follow the FSU Academic Honor Policy process when alleged academic misconduct occurs" binds instructors to the formal integrity process for suspected AI misuse (when-misuse, must); P36 is the integrity-process type.
units.resolution_why: A coded must, B coded should. The source says 'Be sure to follow the FSU Academic Honor Policy process', an unhedged directive to instructors, so must. Actor, phase and type agree.
units.anchor: Be sure to follow the FSU Academic Honor Policy process when alleged academic misconduct occurs.

units.why: The passage states that the Honor Policy "addresses AI-related misconduct such as cheating, plagiarism, and falsification", i.e. AI misuse is handled as academic misconduct (informs, P36).
units.anchor: addresses AI-related misconduct such as cheating, plagiarism, and falsification

units.why: "honors students' rights and due process" says AI-misconduct cases protect student fairness and process; P64 (fairness in AI integrity cases) fits better than the generic P36 since the point is due process.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. The Honor Policy 'honors students' rights and due process' is a policy statement about student rights in misconduct cases, so it is kept. B coded the later 'clear process ... honoring student rights and due process' sentence instead.
units.anchor: honors students’ rights and due process

units.why: Defines cheating via the example of unauthorized AI during an exam; it classifies exam AI misuse as misconduct (P36). P22 would fit only if it banned exam AI outright; here it defines the misconduct.
units.anchor: Use of unauthorized AI tools during an exam is an example of cheating with AI.

units.why: "Presenting AI-generated content as though it is original work is an example of plagiarism" classifies undisclosed AI-produced submissions as plagiarism (P36); P19 states a ban on submission, whereas this defines the misconduct category.
units.anchor: Presenting AI-generated content as though it is original work is an example of plagiarism.

units.why: "use of AI to generate false citations, documents, or signatures" is named as falsification, a form of misconduct, so it is classified under P36.
units.anchor: Examples of falsification include use of AI to generate false citations, documents, or signatures.

units.why: "The ability to hold students accountable ... depends on how clearly you communicate your expectations" gives the reason instructors must state AI expectations; P09 is the closest type since it concerns stating expectations.
units.anchor: The ability to hold students accountable for their use of AI in coursework depends on
units.policy: The ability to hold students accountable for their use of AI in coursework depends on how clearly you communicate your expectations.

units.why: Cites a "2025 survey" by the AI advisory committee finding student anxiety when AI instructions are unclear; this is evidence about AI and students, so P55.
units.resolution_why: Actor: A said all, B said admin. The sentence reports a survey result by the AI in Education Advisory Committee and addresses no one in particular, so all.
units.anchor: students reported high levels of anxiety when instructions for AI use in an assignment were
units.policy: students reported high levels of anxiety when instructions for AI use in an assignment were not clearly communicated

units.why: "Open conversations with students about the acceptable use of AI" is advice to instructors to discuss AI rules, a communication practice (P09 closest).
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. 'Open conversations with students about the acceptable use of AI encourages transparency and accountability' recommends talking with students about acceptable use, so it is kept.
units.anchor: Open conversations with students about the acceptable use of AI

units.why: The same sentence gives a rationale: such conversations prepare students "to apply AI responsibly in future careers and professional environments", a career-preparation rationale (P44).
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all / phase general; B coded instructor / course-start. The clause 'preparing them to apply AI responsibly in future careers' is a rationale for open conversations, not an instruction to a specific instructor at a specific point, so all / general.
units.anchor: preparing them to apply AI responsibly in future careers and professional environments

units.why: "The traffic light framework provides a helpful structure for communicating AI policies" recommends named tiers (traffic light) for syllabi, which is P05.
units.anchor: The traffic light framework provides a helpful structure for communicating AI policies to students.

units.why: The page points to 'example AI use statements that can be copied and adapted for FSU courses', offering templates of tiered statements; P05.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. The page points instructors to 'example AI use statements that can be copied and adapted for FSU courses'; it states a resource instructors may use for tiers, so it is kept.
units.anchor: example AI use statements that can be copied and adapted for FSU courses

units.why: The heading 'Don’t Use AI Detection Tools' is a direct instruction to instructors not to rely on detectors, so P39 with must-not.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this heading. 'Don't Use AI Detection Tools' is the directive in the detector section, which A folded into the next sentence's unit. It is the policy itself, so it is kept as must-not.
units.anchor: Don’t Use AI Detection Tools
units.policy: Instructors do not use AI detection tools to substantiate academic misconduct allegations.

units.why: The sentence 'these tools are not licensed by the university and are highly unreliable' states a fact about AI detectors that grounds the 'Don't Use AI Detection Tools' heading; it is a rationale, so informs, and it belongs under P39 because it explains why detectors are not relied on.
units.resolution_why: A coded must-not with a policy that bundled 'instructors are told not to use detection tools'; B coded informs and put the prohibition in a separate unit on the heading. The source has the heading as the directive and this sentence as the reason, so the reason is informs and the directive is kept as its own unit (only_B).
units.anchor: these tools are not licensed by the university and are highly unreliable
units.policy: AI detectors are not licensed by the university and are highly unreliable.

units.why: Explains detector unreliability: "AI detectors often generate false positives and are subject to hallucination", supporting P39 as a factual claim.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this sentence on false positives and hallucination in AI detectors. B folded it into one unit with the preceding sentence. It states a separate reason detectors are unreliable, so it is kept.
units.anchor: AI detectors often generate false positives and are subject to hallucination

units.why: Warns that content shared with detectors "may be retained by the vendor and used to train its large language model", causing unauthorized disclosure of protected information; a privacy rule, P50.
units.resolution_why: Phase: A said when-misuse, B said general. The vendor-retention warning is given in the paragraph on using detectors to substantiate misconduct allegations, so when-misuse. Actor, modality and type agree.
units.anchor: content shared with them may be retained by the vendor and used to train its
units.policy: content shared with them may be retained by the vendor and used to train its large language model

units.anchor: The university provides all instructors tools to help ensure academic integrity

units.why: 'early intervention is key' with instruction to email FDA then contact the student states the reporting procedure for suspected misconduct; P36.
units.resolution_why: Same passage. A anchored on 'early intervention is key' and B on 'the best approach is to email FDA-AcademicIntegrity@fsu.edu, then promptly contact the student'. Codes agree; the final unit uses B's anchor and normalized policy because it states the concrete rule.
units.anchor: the best approach is to email
units.frag_start: When it comes to addressing alleged
units.policy: When misconduct is suspected, the instructor emails FDA-AcademicIntegrity@fsu.edu and then promptly contacts the student once an FDA administrator responds, rather than waiting to gather enough evidence.

units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. 'The university provides a clear process to address suspected misconduct ... honoring student rights and due process' is a separate sentence from the earlier Honor Policy line, so it is kept.
units.anchor: honoring student rights and due process
units.frag_start: The university provides a clear process
units.policy: The university provides a clear process for suspected misconduct that promotes academic integrity while honoring student rights and due process.

units.resolution_why: A coded must, B coded should. 'Email ... to determine if the student has had a previous violation' is the instruction under 'As Soon As You Suspect Misconduct', stated without hedging, so must.
units.anchor: to determine if the student has had a previous violation

units.anchor: Before talking with your student, review the AI use expectations you included in your syllabus,
units.policy: Before talking with your student, review the AI use expectations you included in your syllabus, assignment instructions, and Canvas course site.

units.why: 'Gather any documentation and create a brief timeline of the suspected misconduct' is a preparation step before the conversation with the student, so it is P57 (gather context before escalating), not P40: the passage is not about similarity checks or process evidence tools.
units.resolution_why: A coded P40, B coded P57. The sentence sits under 'Preparing for the Conversation' and tells instructors to gather context before talking to the student, which matches P57. The following sentence about cross-referencing links stays P40 (both coders), since it uses evidence checking.
units.anchor: Gather any documentation and create a brief timeline of the suspected misconduct.

units.why: Because AI "can produce hallucinations and incorrect or broken links", instructors should cross-reference student citations; this is a verification step for evidence (P40).
units.anchor: cross-reference links and other information (eg, citations) the student provides

units.why: The instructor should schedule an 'in-person meeting or meet virtually using a university-licensed web conferencing tool', part of talking with the student before escalation; P57.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. 'schedule an in-person meeting or meet virtually using a university-licensed web conferencing tool' is a distinct instruction on how to meet the student, so it is kept.
units.anchor: schedule an in-person meeting or meet virtually using a university-licensed web conferencing tool

units.anchor: Do not record meetings

units.why: "use open-ended questions to explore and address the allegations" after acknowledging circumstances tells instructors to hear the student out before escalation (P57).
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. 'use open-ended questions to explore and address the allegations' is a separate instruction from asking for evidence of effort, so it is kept; B merged both into one unit.
units.anchor: use open-ended questions to explore and address the allegations

units.why: 'Ask for evidence of effort and learning outside of class, pointing out gaps in the student's explanations' is advice for the conversation about allegations, so it is P57; P34 (oral exams, interviews as assessment) does not fit because this is an investigatory talk, not an assessment.
units.resolution_why: A coded P34, B coded P57. The passage is under 'Discussing Allegations' and describes how to talk with the student about suspected misuse, not how to assess understanding, so P57.

units.policy: Ask for evidence of effort and learning outside of class, pointing out gaps in the student’s explanations.

units.why: 'write detailed notes summarizing the discussion and send them to your student within 48 hours' is the follow-up step of the instructor's conversation with the student, so P57; P64 (right to respond) is not stated here.
units.resolution_why: A coded P64, B coded P57. The notes follow the conversation and are sent to the student, but the passage does not give the student a right to respond or present evidence; that appears in the separate resolution-options email (coded P64). So P57.
units.anchor: write detailed notes summarizing the discussion and send them to your student within 48 hours

units.why: The instructor 'offers the resolution options your student is eligible to pursue per the Academic Honor Policy', so students are informed of their options; P64.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. The separate email offering resolution options the student can pursue is a distinct step that gives the student a route to respond, so it is kept as P64.
units.anchor: offers the resolution options your student is eligible to pursue
units.frag_start: When a discussion supports the allegations
units.policy: When a discussion supports the allegations, the instructor sends the student a separate email describing unresolved concerns and offering the resolution options the student is eligible to pursue under the Academic Honor Policy.

units.why: 'prioritize proposed sanctions that educate and remediate, not merely penalize' states a sanction principle but no concrete penalty and not classification as misconduct, so no existing type fits.
units.resolution_why: A coded P36, B coded UNCOVERED. 'prioritize proposed sanctions that educate and remediate, not merely penalize' is a principle about the purpose of sanctions. P36 (classify unauthorized use as misconduct) and P37 (state concrete penalties) do not say this, so UNCOVERED is kept and counted as a codebook finding.
units.anchor: prioritize proposed sanctions that educate and remediate, not merely penalize
units.frag_start: It is always a best practice to prioritize
units.policy: Instructors prioritize proposed sanctions that educate and remediate, not merely penalize.
units.uncovered_note: Sanction philosophy: prefer educative and remedial sanctions over purely punitive ones.

units.why: "be prepared to compile documentation ... and forward it to FDA" is a step in the Academic Honor Policy process when a discussion supports allegations (P36).
units.anchor: compile documentation (eg, your syllabus, all evidence, notes, timeline of event, completed Academic Honor Policy
units.policy: compile documentation (eg, your syllabus, all evidence, notes, timeline of event, completed Academic Honor Policy resolution form)
